overview: The Pechenegs were a Turkic confederation whose herders, traders and warriors became major neighbours of Rus and Byzantium. Their activity extended across the steppe between the Don and Danube. This imported map covers only 900 to 1000 and shows a small northern fragment: it leaves out much of their historical range and does not mark the limits of a compact kingdom.

periods.title: The mapped tenth-century phase
periods.summary: A major steppe confederation; its history continued beyond this map interval.

items.text: In 972, Pechenegs killed Prince Sviatoslav of Kyiv near the Dnipro rapids. Control of these difficult crossings could interrupt journeys between the northern river towns and the Black Sea. Steppe politics mattered far beyond the grasslands.

Constantine VII’s tenth-century handbook says Rus bought cattle, horses and sheep from the Pechenegs. It also describes the danger of attacks when travellers hauled boats around river obstacles. The same neighbours could supply livestock in peacetime and threaten a trading journey during war.

The handbook also describes Pechenegs negotiating payment for services to people from Cherson in Crimea. The list includes textiles and pepper. Diplomacy and paid work could bring goods from distant markets into steppe life; pepper was part of the bargain, not evidence of a surviving Pecheneg recipe.

Historian Aleksander Paroń reconstructs seasonal movement between northern summer grazing and more sheltered southern winter pastures. This uses comparisons with other steppe herders as well as written evidence. Moving camp followed the needs of animals and grass, rather than a random search for somewhere new.

In Paroń’s reconstruction, milk availability changed sharply through the year. Animals weakened by winter gave little milk in late winter and early spring, while summer offered more dairy food. A household’s menu depended partly on the season of its herd.

Paroń describes leather footwear and bags, sewing with animal-tendon thread, and wool felt used over yurts. These household skills turned herd products into shelter and useful containers. The reconstruction draws partly on comparative evidence, so these are carefully assembled clues to household life rather than an inventory from one excavated home.

Bone plates from composite bows occur in burial assemblages discussed by Paroń. They are physical traces of working bone and horn for equipment that combined different materials. A skilled rider’s weapons depended on craft knowledge as well as practice on horseback.

sections.title: Later discoveries around the lower Danube

items.text: A later, eleventh-century grave at Histria, excavated in 1972 among Roman bath ruins, contained two openwork leaf-shaped pendants beside a woman’s jaw and eleven coloured glass beads. They probably formed a necklace. Such ornaments enter debates about Pecheneg connections, but the jewellery alone cannot establish the woman’s identity.

A fragmentary lead casting model found in the Roman baths at Varna suggests that similar leaf-shaped ornaments could be produced in the northern Balkans. Florin Curta considers local manufacture and changing fashions when interpreting them. An attractive pendant could travel as an idea as well as an object.

Curta also questions the habit of treating every clay kettle as a Pecheneg ethnic marker. These vessels occur in settled communities, and their distribution does not neatly match the people described in written sources. Archaeologists must compare dates, places and contexts before turning a pot into a population map.

A 2024 study by Rosen and Rumen Ivanov examines Bulgarian pottery they associate with Pechenegs. Cooking vessels outnumber tableware. Their earliest northeastern examples date to the 1030s and 1040s, with southeastern examples later in the eleventh century. This evidence concerns life after the atlas’s tenth-century slice, as communities entered Balkan settlements and fortresses.

sections.title: A name in a neighbouring writer’s language

items.text: A heading in Constantine VII’s handbook reads “Περὶ τῶν Πατζινακιτῶν”, meaning “About the Pechenegs”. The sample comes from a modern transcription of his mid-tenth-century Greek work. It preserves a Byzantine writer’s name for the people, rather than a Pecheneg-language sentence or a specimen of their own handwriting.

ending.text: Defeat near Kyiv in 1036 and pressure from other steppe groups helped redirect Pecheneg power toward the Balkans. Byzantine victories in 1091 and 1122 ended major independent military formations. Survivors entered other societies and armies, including those of Hungary and Rus. The map’s 1000 endpoint is not their disappearance.
